Recognizing concentration-related toxicity

A 45-year-old man taking phenytoin presents after a recent dose adjustment. He is awake but has horizontal nystagmus, slurred speech and a broad-based unsteady gait. There is no unilateral weakness. Which explanation best fits this pattern?

  1. An isolated peripheral neuromuscular-junction block
  2. A pure antimuscarinic syndrome
  3. Therapeutic activation of dopamine receptors
  4. Expected proof that seizure control is optimal
  5. Concentration-related phenytoin neurotoxicity
Answer and explanation

Concentration-related phenytoin neurotoxicity

Nystagmus, dysarthria and ataxia are characteristic neurologic manifestations of excessive phenytoin exposure.

Option explanations

Concentration-related phenytoin neurotoxicity: Nystagmus, dysarthria and ataxia are characteristic neurologic manifestations of excessive phenytoin exposure.

An isolated peripheral neuromuscular-junction block: This would not characteristically produce nystagmus with cerebellar signs.

A pure antimuscarinic syndrome: Dry skin, mydriasis and urinary retention would be more characteristic.

Therapeutic activation of dopamine receptors: Phenytoin is not a dopamine agonist.

Expected proof that seizure control is optimal: Toxic neurologic signs are not a marker of optimal treatment.
